IB Chemistry HL
Reaction of Chloromethane with Hydroxide Ion

How do I use this resource?

a

i

medium

Using Graph 1, deduce the value of ΔT\Delta TΔT for this reaction. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

ai

Mark Scheme

ΔT=8 ∘C ✓\Delta T = 8\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} \: \checkmarkΔT=8∘C✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The reaction is exothermic, but it does not occur instantaneously and heat is lost to the surroundings throughout. The temperature therefore rises to a maximum and then falls, once the rate of heat loss exceeds the rate at which the reaction releases heat. That maximum is lower than the temperature the mixture would have reached had no heat escaped, so using it directly would make the calculated enthalpy change too small.

Extrapolating the straight line through the cooling data back to the time of mixing corrects for this loss. Here the extrapolated temperature is 33 ∘C33\,{}^\circ\textrm{C}33∘C and the initial temperature is 25 ∘C,25\,{}^\circ\textrm{C},25∘C, giving

ΔT=33 ∘C−25 ∘C=8 ∘C\Delta T = 33\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} - 25\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} = \answer{8\,{}^\circ\textrm{C}}ΔT=33∘C−25∘C=8∘C​

 \  

ii

hard

Using the parameters in Table 1, calculate the value of SSS in the Experimental Model, including its units. [3]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

aii

Mark Scheme

V=100+100=200 cm3 ✓V = 100 + 100 = 200 \textrm{\ cm}^3 \: \checkmarkV=100+100=200 cm3✓
S=200×0.786=157 ✓S = 200 \times 0.786 = 157 \: \checkmarkS=200×0.786=157✓
units: g\textrm{g}g / grams ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The units of SSS follow from the rest of the equation. The heat capacity ccc is given in J K−1 g−1,\textrm{J K}^{-1} \textrm{\ g}^{-1},J K−1 g−1, so cΔTc\Delta TcΔT has units of J g−1,\textrm{J g}^{-1},J g−1, and dividing by 1000 converts this to kJ g−1.\textrm{kJ g}^{-1}.kJ g−1. That is an energy per gram, so multiplying by SSS yields an energy in kJ only if SSS is the mass of the reaction mixture in grams.

The two solutions are mixed, so the volume of the mixture is 100+100=200 cm3.100 + 100 = 200 \textrm{\ cm}^3.100+100=200 cm3. Multiplying by the density gives

S=200 cm3×0.786 g cm−3=157 gS = 200 \textrm{\ cm}^3 \times 0.786 \textrm{\ g cm}^{-3} = \answer{157 \textrm{\ g}}S=200 cm3×0.786 g cm−3=157 g​

The molar masses and the amount of chloromethane in the table are not needed here; they are used at the next stage, when the energy released is divided by the amount of limiting reactant.

iii

medium

Calculate the value of ΔHr,\Delta H_r,ΔHr​, in kJ mol−1\textrm{kJ mol}^{-1}kJ mol−1 using the Experimental Model. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

ΔHr=−56.0 kJ mol−1 ✓\Delta H_r =-56.0 \textrm{\ kJ mol}^{-1} \: \checkmarkΔHr​=−56.0 kJ mol−1✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
Substituting the extrapolated temperature change and the mass of the reaction mixture into the equation gives the energy released per mole of chloromethane. The negative sign is already built into the equation and records that the reaction is exothermic: the mixture warms because energy is transferred out of the reacting system.

ΔHr=−2.23 J g−1K−1×8 K1000 J kJ−1×0.0500 mol×157 g=−56.0 kJ mol−1\Delta H_r = -\dfrac{2.23 \textrm{\ J g}^{-1}\textrm{K}^{-1} \times 8 \textrm{\ K}}{1000 \textrm{\ J kJ}^{-1} \times 0.0500 \textrm{\ mol}} \times 157 \textrm{\ g} = \answer{-56.0 \textrm{\ kJ mol}^{-1}}ΔHr​=−1000 J kJ−1×0.0500 mol2.23 J g−1K−1×8 K​×157 g=−56.0 kJ mol−1​

The value is quoted per mole of chloromethane because chloromethane is the limiting reactant. The two solutions have equal volumes, but the hydroxide is twice as concentrated, so hydroxide ions are in excess and some remain unreacted when the chloromethane is used up.

iv

hard

In a second experiment, the volume of hydroxide solution was halved, and the concentration was doubled. The volume and concentration of the chloromethane solution were not changed. The measured value of ΔT\Delta TΔT was larger than in the first experiment.

Suggest why a larger value of ΔT\Delta TΔT was measured. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

aiv

Mark Scheme

mass / volume of the reaction mixture is smaller ✓\checkmark✓
same amount of energy is released, so each gram of mixture absorbs more energy; ΔT\Delta TΔT is larger ✓\checkmark✓

Do not award M2 unless the larger ΔT\Delta TΔT is linked to the smaller quantity of reaction mixture.

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
Halving the volume of the hydroxide solution while doubling its concentration leaves the amount of hydroxide unchanged, and the chloromethane is untouched. The same amount of reaction therefore occurs and the same quantity of energy is released.

That energy is now shared among a smaller mass of solution. The total volume falls from 200 cm3200 \textrm{\ cm}^3200 cm3 to 150 cm3,150 \textrm{\ cm}^3,150 cm3, three−-−quarters of the original, so SSS falls in the same proportion. With ΔHr\Delta H_rΔHr​ and nnn unchanged, ΔT\Delta TΔT must rise by a factor of 43.\frac{4}{3}.34​.

b

i

hard

Suggest why the calculated yield may not be reliable based on the information in Graph 2. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

bi

Mark Scheme

signals are not baseline−-−resolved / peaks overlap at base, so limits of each integral are uncertain ✓\checkmark✓
OR
product signal is small, so uncertainty in integration limits is a large fraction of its integral ✓\checkmark✓

Accept: the reactant signal is larger, so including a small part of its area in the product integral causes an overestimate of the calculated yield.

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The integral of a signal is the area between the baseline and the curve, and is proportional to the number of protons in that environment. Measuring it requires a decision about where the signal begins and ends. Here the trace does not return to the baseline between the two peaks, so that decision is a judgement rather than a measurement, and different choices of limit give different integrals.

The consequence falls unevenly. The chloromethane signal is much the larger of the two, so a small part of its area counted into the methanol integral shifts the product integral by a large proportion while barely affecting the reactant. The yield calculated from the product signal is therefore sensitive to where the boundary is drawn, and is likely to be overestimated.

ii

medium

State whether the error described in (i) is random or systematic, giving a reason for your answer. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

bii

Mark Scheme

systematic ✓\checkmark✓

repeating analysis gives same overlap, same excess area is added to product integral each time ✓\checkmark✓
OR
two signals always appear at the same chemical shifts, so product integral is inflated by same amount in every measurement ✓\checkmark✓

Do not award M2 for a general definition of systematic error.

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
A random error displaces individual measurements unpredictably, so repeats scatter above and below the true value and averaging reduces the effect. A systematic error displaces every measurement in the same direction, so averaging does not help.

Re−-−running the spectrum on the same mixture reproduces the same two overlapping signals, so the same reactant area is counted into the product integral every time. The yield is overestimated in every repeat, which is what makes the error systematic rather than random.

medium

The calculated yield after 1 min1 \textrm{\ min}1 min was 0.084±0.003 mol dm−3.0.084\pm 0.003\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}.0.084±0.003mol dm−3.

Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the calculated yield. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

biii

Mark Scheme

% uncertainty = 4% ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The percentage uncertainty is the ratio of the absolute uncertainty to the measured quantity:

% uncertainty=0.003 mol dm−30.084 mol dm−3×100%=4%\textrm{\% uncertainty} = \dfrac{0.003 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}}{0.084 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}} \times 100\% = \answer{4\%}% uncertainty=0.084 mol dm−30.003 mol dm−3​×100%=4%​

Introduction
​

Introduction

When a hydroxide salt is added to a solution of chloromethane in an organic solvent, an exothermic reaction occurs. The equation for this reaction is shown.

 \  

Graph 1: Calorimetry Curve

The enthalpy change of the reaction, ΔHr,\Delta H_r,ΔHr​, was measured by performing the reaction in a calorimeter.

Graph 1: 100 cm3100\,\text{cm}^3100cm3 solution of hydroxide ions (1.00 mol dm−3)(1.00\,\text{mol dm}^{-3})(1.00mol dm−3) was added rapidly to 100 cm3100\,\text{cm}^3100cm3 chloromethane (0.50 mol dm−3),(0.50\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}),(0.50mol dm−3), stirred, and the temperature of the mixture was measured as a function of time.

Experimental Model

The value of ΔHr,\Delta H_r,ΔHr​, in kJ mol−1,\text{kJ mol}^{-1},kJ mol−1, is calculated using the equation

ΔHr=(−cΔT1000 n)(S)\Delta H_r = \left(\dfrac{-c \Delta T}{1000\, n}\right)(S)ΔHr​=(1000n−cΔT​)(S)

 \  

Table 1: Parameters

ParameterSymbolValueUnits
Heat capacity of reaction mixtureccc2.23J K−1 g−1\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{g}^{-1}J K−1g−1
Moles of chloromethanennn0.0500mol
Volume of hydroxide solution100cm3\text{cm}^3cm3
Volume of chloromethane solution100cm3\text{cm}^3cm3
Density of reaction mixture0.786g cm−3\text{g cm}^{-3}g cm−3
Molar mass of solvent41.1g mol−1\text{g mol}^{-1}g mol−1
Molar mass of chloromethane50.5g mol−1\text{g mol}^{-1}g mol−1

Table 1: Parameters that may be used in the calculation of the enthalpy change.

Graph 2: NMR

The reaction mixture was sampled after 1 min1\,\text{min}1min and analyzed by X1X221H\ce{^1H}X1​X221​H NMR spectroscopy. The resulting spectrum contains two strong signals corresponding to the CHX3\ce{CH3}CHX3​ protons of the product and unreacted chloromethane, as shown. The integral of the product signal at 3.065 ppm3.065 \textrm{\ ppm}3.065 ppm was used to calculate the yield of the reaction after 1 min.1\,\text{min}.1min.

Graph 2: 1^11H NMR of the reaction mixture after 1 minute.
